results.result: Persistent Na+ influx through TTX-insensitive conductance contributes to subthreshold depolarization in VTA DA neurons. Replacing extracellular Ca2+ with Mg2+ increased firing frequency and did not hyperpolarize RMP, while replacing Na+ with NMDG hyperpolarized RMP, indicating Ca2+ influx is not necessary but Na+ influx is critical for spontaneous firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C32 provide converging experimental evidence with appropriate statistical tests showing that Ca2+ removal increases firing (p<0.0001) while Na+ removal hyperpolarizes RMP (p<0.0001). The experimental design includes proper controls and the conclusions are directly supported by the data. Claims C86-C87 provide appropriate context from prior work.

results.result: Single-cell RNA-seq of projection-specific VTA DA neurons reveals expression profiles of neurotransmitter markers and non-selective cation channels. Among NSCCs, Trpc6 shows projection-specific expression with higher levels in NAc-projecting neurons compared to BLA- and mPFC-projecting neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C40 are supported by RNA-seq data (Figure 2) showing DA neuron markers, glutamatergic/GABAergic co-expression patterns, and NSCC expression profiles. The projection-specific expression of Trpc6 (C40) is clearly demonstrated. Sample sizes (60 neurons from 5 projection targets) appear adequate for this exploratory analysis.

results.result: HCN channels do not contribute to spontaneous firing in adult VTA DA neurons despite effectively reducing sag potentials. HCN blockers (CsCl and ZD7288) had no significant effect on firing frequency in adult mice, but did reduce firing in young mice (<15d postnatal), suggesting age-dependent changes in HCN function.
results.evaluation: Claims C41-C48 provide comprehensive evidence with appropriate controls showing HCN blockers reduce sag potentials (p<0.05) but not firing frequency (p>0.05) in adult mice. The age-dependent effect (C47, p=0.0101) and hyperpolarization experiments (C45-C46) support the conclusion that depolarized RMP prevents HCN involvement in adult neurons. Statistical tests are appropriate.

results.result: NALCN is a major contributor to subthreshold depolarization and spontaneous firing in VTA DA neurons. Both pharmacological blockers (GdCl3 and L703,606) and genetic knockdown of NALCN significantly hyperpolarized RMP and reduced/silenced spontaneous firing.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C57 provide converging evidence from pharmacology (p<0.01 for both blockers) and genetics (shRNA knockdown with qPCR validation, p=0.004). The near-complete silencing of firing (0.08±0.02 Hz vs 1.60±0.15 Hz, p<0.0001) and RMP hyperpolarization (p<0.0001) strongly support NALCN's role. Multiple experimental approaches strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: TRPC6 is an important contributor to subthreshold depolarization and spontaneous firing in VTA DA neurons. Single-cell PCR confirmed high expression (64.3% of DA neurons), pharmacological blockers (2-APB and LA) significantly reduced firing and hyperpolarized RMP, and genetic knockdown substantially reduced firing frequency and hyperpolarized RMP. TRPC6 shows projection-specific expression with lower levels in mPFC-projecting neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C71 provide comprehensive evidence from expression analysis, pharmacology (p<0.001 for both blockers), and genetics (knockdown reduces firing from 1.88±0.16 to 0.43±0.07 Hz, p<0.0001). The loss of blocker effects after knockdown (C69-C70, p>0.15) confirms specificity. TRPC3 absence (C59) strengthens the case for TRPC6-specific effects. Statistical tests are appropriate throughout.

results.result: In CMUS and CRS depression models, TRPC6 protein is downregulated in VTA and VTA DA neuron firing frequency is reduced. TRP channel blockers show diminished effects in CMUS mice compared to controls, consistent with TRPC6 downregulation. NALCN protein levels were unchanged in CMUS mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C79 demonstrate consistent findings across two depression models (CMUS and CRS). Behavioral validation (C72), reduced firing (C73, p<0.0001), TRPC6 downregulation in both models (C74, C76, p<0.0001), and reduced blocker efficacy (C77-C78) provide converging evidence. The unchanged NALCN (C75) serves as an appropriate negative control. Sample sizes are adequate (N=10-33 mice).

results.result: Selective knockdown of TRPC6 in VTA DA neurons induces depression- and anxiety-like behaviors in mice. Cre-dependent knockdown in Slc6a3-Cre mice reduced sucrose preference, increased immobility time, and reduced open arm exploration. TRPC6 overexpression rescued these behavioral deficits. Projection-specific knockdown in mPFC-projecting neurons also induced depression/anxiety behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C80-C85 provide strong causal evidence linking TRPC6 to behavior. Multiple behavioral tests show consistent effects (p<0.01 for all measures), rescue experiments (C83) demonstrate specificity, and projection-specific manipulations (C84) identify circuit mechanisms. The experimental design with Cre-dependent approaches is rigorous. Sample sizes (N=10 per group) are adequate for behavioral studies.

results.result: VTA DA neurons are slow intrinsic pacemakers that project to multiple brain regions (NAc, mPFC, BLA) and modulate target circuits through regulated firing activity. Altered VTA DA neuron activity is a key determinant in depression and anxiety-related behaviors.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2 and C8-C13 establish the background context with appropriate citations. These are well-established facts in the field supported by the cited literature. The claims provide necessary context for interpreting the experimental findings but do not represent novel findings from this study.

results.result: Various ion channels regulate spontaneous firing in midbrain DA neurons, but the specific channels mediating subthreshold depolarization in VTA DA neurons remain incompletely characterized. HCN channels show controversial results, NALCN is a candidate for Na+ leak currents, and TRP channels (particularly TRPC3 in SNc) have been implicated in neuronal excitability.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C27 accurately summarize prior literature with appropriate citations, identifying knowledge gaps that motivate the current study. These background claims are well-supported by the cited references and establish the rationale for investigating NALCN and TRPC6 in VTA DA neurons.

results.result: NALCN and TRPC6 mediate subthreshold inward depolarizing current and drive action potential firing in VTA DA neurons under physiological conditions. Down-regulation of TRPC6 contributes to reduced VTA DA neuron activity in CMUS mice and depression-like behavior.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C7 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the detailed experimental evidence in the grouped results above. These summary claims integrate findings from pharmacology, genetics, electrophysiology, and behavior experiments. The evidence is comprehensive and internally consistent.

results.result: TRPC6 and TRPC3 are highly homologous (>75%), and TRPC6's role in subthreshold depolarization likely involves persistent Na+ permeation. The TRPC6 activator hyperforin is an effective antidepressant and the principal component of St. John's wort, suggesting TRPC6 as a drug target for antidepressants.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C93 provide appropriate context from prior literature (with citations) and draw reasonable conclusions about therapeutic implications. The homology claim (C89) is factual, the mechanistic inference (C90) is reasonable given TRPC6's known properties, and the therapeutic potential (C91-C93) is supported by cited studies. However, direct testing of TRPC6 activators was not performed in this study.

results.result: The authors demonstrate that persistent Na+ influx through TTX-insensitive conductance contributes to subthreshold depolarization in VTA DA neurons. Replacing extracellular Ca2+ with Mg2+ increased firing frequency and did not hyperpolarize RMP, while replacing Na+ with NMDG caused significant hyperpolarization, indicating Na+ influx drives subthreshold depolarization.
results.evaluation: Multiple reviewers explicitly affirm these neurophysiological findings. One reviewer states the authors' 'conclusions on neurophysiological data are supported by multiple approaches and are convincing.' Another notes 'the authors have responded satisfactorily to reviewer comments, and the revised manuscript is improved,' indicating acceptance of the ion substitution experiments and their interpretation.

results.result: NALCN is identified as a major contributor to subthreshold depolarization and spontaneous firing in VTA DA neurons. Both pharmacological blockers (GdCl3 and L703,606) and genetic knockdown of NALCN significantly hyperpolarized RMP and reduced or silenced spontaneous firing.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly support these findings as a key mechanism. One reviewer describes the study as examining 'NALCN and TRPC6 channels as key mechanisms that regulate spontaneous firing' and states the neurophysiological conclusions are 'convincing.' The use of 'multiple approaches' including pharmacology and knockdown is noted as a strength.

results.result: TRPC6 is identified as an important contributor to subthreshold depolarization and spontaneous firing in VTA DA neurons, with projection-specific expression patterns. RNA-seq and single-cell PCR showed prominent Trpc6 expression, with higher levels in NAc-projecting neurons. Pharmacological blockers (2-APB, LA) and genetic knockdown reduced firing and hyperpolarized RMP, effects that were diminished in TRPC6-knockdown neurons.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm these findings as part of the key mechanisms identified. One reviewer explicitly states the authors 'identify NALCN and TRPC6 channels as key mechanisms regulating VTA dopaminergic neuron spontaneous firing' and notes the 'multiple approaches' strengthen the conclusions. The neurophysiological data are described as 'convincing.'

results.result: HCN channels are not involved in spontaneous firing of adult VTA DA neurons under physiological conditions, despite effectively reducing sag potential. HCN blockers (CsCl, ZD7288) did not significantly inhibit spontaneous firing in adult mice, though ZD7288 reduced firing in young mice and under hyperpolarized conditions (low K+).
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge these findings about HCN channels. The comprehensive approach using multiple conditions and age groups is consistent with the reviewers' acknowledgment that the study uses 'multiple approaches' and that the neurophysiological conclusions are 'supported' and 'convincing.'

results.result: In CMUS depression model mice, VTA DA neuron firing frequency was significantly reduced, accompanied by down-regulation of TRPC6 protein (but not NALCN). The inhibitory effects of TRPC6 blockers on mPFC-projecting VTA DA neurons were diminished in CMUS mice compared to controls, suggesting TRPC6 down-regulation contributes to altered firing in depression.
results.evaluation: Reviewers affirm the study 'examined their roles in reduced firing in mice that underwent a chronic mild unpredictable stress treatment' and that conclusions are 'supported by multiple approaches.' The Western blot and electrophysiology data linking TRPC6 downregulation to reduced firing are accepted as part of the convincing neurophysiological findings.

results.result: Selective knockdown of TRPC6 in VTA DA neurons (particularly mPFC-projecting neurons) induced depression- and anxiety-like behaviors in mice, including reduced sucrose preference, increased immobility time, and reduced open arm exploration. TRPC6 overexpression rescued these behavioral deficits, establishing a causal link between TRPC6 down-regulation and depression/anxiety phenotypes.
results.evaluation: While reviewers accept the neurophysiological data as 'convincing,' one reviewer explicitly states 'the relevance of the behavioral results to human depression remains unclear.' Another reviewer notes the tasks 'mainly address anxiety-like behaviors and so-called depression-like behaviors' with emphasis on 'so-called,' suggesting reservations about interpreting these rodent behaviors as modeling human depression. The behavioral findings are acknowledged but their translational relevance is questioned.

results.result: RNA-seq characterization of projection-specific VTA DA neurons showed that 45/60 sequenced neurons expressed DA markers (Th, Ddc, Slc6a3), with some co-expressing glutamatergic markers (Slc17a6-8) and fewer expressing GABAergic markers (Gad1/2, Slc32a1). VTA DA neurons projecting to different brain regions are anatomically segregated into VTA subregions.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge the RNA-seq characterization or anatomical findings. The use of 'multiple approaches' is noted as a strength, and the molecular profiling supports the subsequent mechanistic studies that reviewers found convincing.

results.result: Ruthenium Red (RR, 60 μM), a TRPV blocker, did not statistically affect spontaneous firing of VTA DA neurons on average, though individual neurons showed variable responses.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this negative finding. It serves as a control supporting the specificity of TRPC6 effects and is consistent with the RNA-seq data showing TRPV2 expression but lack of functional contribution under the conditions tested.

results.result: Unlike SNc DA neurons where Ca2+ influx is needed for spontaneous firing, Ca2+ influx is not necessary for spontaneous firing of VTA DA neurons. Removing extracellular Ca2+ did not hyperpolarize RMP, verifying the limited role of Ca2+ influx in subthreshold depolarization.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accept these findings as part of the neurophysiological characterization. The comparison to SNc neurons and the mechanistic distinction are not challenged and support the focus on Na+-permeable channels (NALCN, TRPC6) rather than Ca2+ channels.

results.result: VTA DA neurons in adult mice do not use HCN channels to depolarize the membrane to generate action potentials, due to depolarized RMP and hyperpolarization-shifted activation properties.
results.evaluation: This conclusion is supported by the experimental data on HCN blockers and is not challenged by reviewers. It clarifies the mechanistic basis for spontaneous firing and is consistent with the reviewers' acceptance of the neurophysiological findings.

results.result: TRPC6 and TRPC3 are highly homologous (>75%), and TRPC6's role in subthreshold depolarization comes from its contribution through persistent Na+ permeation.
results.evaluation: Reviewers do not challenge this mechanistic interpretation. The homology is cited from literature, and the proposed mechanism of Na+ permeation is consistent with the accepted experimental findings on ion substitution and TRPC6 knockdown effects.

results.result: TRPC6 is proposed as an attractive drug target for antidepressants, based on evidence that TRPC6 activator hyperforin (the principal component of St. John's wort) is effective in multiple depression models.
results.evaluation: While the mechanistic data on TRPC6 are accepted, one reviewer explicitly questions 'the relevance of the behavioral results to human depression,' which directly impacts the translational claim about TRPC6 as a drug target. The connection between rodent behavioral assays and human depression is viewed with uncertainty, limiting confidence in the therapeutic implications.

comparisons.comparison: Perfect agreement on NALCN's role in spontaneous firing (C50-C57). Both evaluations find the evidence convincing, with peer reviewers explicitly noting the 'multiple approaches' including pharmacology and knockdown strengthen the conclusions. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Complete agreement on stress model findings (C72-C79). Both evaluations support the evidence linking TRPC6 downregulation to reduced firing in depression models. Peer reviewers accept the Western blot and electrophysiology data as part of convincing neurophysiological findings. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Divergent evaluations on behavioral findings (C80-C85). OpenEval finds strong causal evidence with rigorous experimental design (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers question the translational relevance, noting 'the relevance of the behavioral results to human depression remains unclear' and expressing reservations about 'so-called depression-like behaviors' (UNCERTAIN).

Strong agreement on HCN channel findings (C41-C48). Both evaluations support the comprehensive evidence showing age-dependent effects and limited role in adult neurons. Peer reviewers acknowledge the multiple approaches and do not challenge these findings. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on TRPC6 mechanism (C58-C71 overlap with C38-C40, C58-C71). Both evaluations find the pharmacological, genetic, and expression evidence convincing. Peer reviewers explicitly affirm TRPC6 as a 'key mechanism' with 'multiple approaches' strengthening conclusions. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Partial disagreement on therapeutic implications (C89-C93). OpenEval supports the mechanistic reasoning and therapeutic potential (SUPPORTED), while peer reviewers accept the mechanism (C89-C90) but question the translational relevance to human depression (C91-C93), rating therapeutic claims as UNCERTAIN.

Agreement on RNA-seq characterization (C34-C37 overlap). Both evaluations support the molecular profiling and anatomical findings. Peer reviewers note the 'multiple approaches' as a strength and do not challenge the characterization. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Strong agreement on ion substitution experiments (C28-C32, with C3-C4 main conclusions). Both evaluations find the neurophysiological data convincing with appropriate controls. Peer reviewers explicitly state conclusions are 'supported by multiple approaches and are convincing.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on mechanistic interpretation (C89-C90). Both evaluations accept the homology claim and proposed Na+ permeation mechanism as consistent with experimental findings. Peer reviewers do not challenge this interpretation. Both rate as SUPPORTED for these specific mechanistic claims.

Agreement on Ca2+ channel findings (C86-C87). Both evaluations accept these contextual findings comparing VTA to SNc neurons. Peer reviewers do not challenge the mechanistic distinction supporting focus on Na+-permeable channels. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on main conclusions (C3-C4 overlap with C28-C32). OpenEval finds the summary claims well-supported by comprehensive evidence, while peer reviewers explicitly affirm the neurophysiological conclusions as 'convincing.' Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on projection-specific TRPC6 expression (C38-C40). Both evaluations support the RNA-seq findings on TRPC6 expression patterns. Peer reviewers affirm TRPC6 as a 'key mechanism' and accept the molecular characterization. Both rate as SUPPORTED.

Agreement on HCN mechanism conclusion (C88). Both evaluations support the conclusion that HCN channels do not drive spontaneous firing in adult VTA neurons. Peer reviewers accept this finding as part of the convincing neurophysiological data. Both rate as SUPPORTED.
